# Product

`customer_support.offering.product` · offering_family · parent `—`

> Something built once and sold many times. The support consequence of "many times" is that demand is a population rather than a series of individuals: the same defect arrives from forty customers who have never met, and the fortieth ticket carries no information the first one did not. That makes the aggregate — not the ticket — the unit of intelligence, and it makes a fix an asset. Labour spent once retires a whole class of future contact, so the marginal cost of the forty-first resolution is zero and the economics reward elimination over service quality. This is the only offering family where the correct long-run goal of a support organisation is to receive less work. The habit an operator carries in from services and gets punished for is treating each ticket as bespoke and answering it beautifully in private. Forty excellent private answers is a failure that looks exactly like excellent work on every dashboard: the article was never written, the issue was never filed, nothing was routed to whoever could make it stop, and next month it is eighty.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | the identical artefact reaches every buyer; value sits in possession or in use rather than in an engagement |
| pricing_shape | recurring subscription, per-unit purchase or licence — priced per copy, never per hour |
| margin_profile | high gross margin with support as the dominant variable cost, which is why cost-to-serve is a board-level number here and a rounding error in services |
| post_sale_load | value is consumed continuously after purchase, so the relationship is never finished and there is no point at which the revenue is safe |
| support_load | correlated across the install base and event-driven — one bad release, one expired certificate, one changed third-party API turns a queue into a spike within the hour. Steady-state volume tracks active users, not revenue, which is why the cheapest segment is usually the loudest |
| resolution_locus | the artefact itself in the general case — but WHICH artefact and who is permitted to touch it is exactly what separates the four types below. A fix we deploy, a fix we put in a van, a fix the customer must install and a fix that is really a refund are four different jobs wearing one word |
| notes | The commercially useful test for whether something is a product in the support sense is not how it is priced but whether the fix is reusable. Software billed per hour is still a product to support if the same code change helps the next customer.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `issue_ref`, `product_area_ref`


> A product ticket that does not link to an underlying issue and a product area cannot be aggregated, and an unaggregatable product queue can answer "how busy are we" but never "what should we fix". These two fields are what make the sentence "forty customers hit this" expressible at all; without them every report is a fresh surprise and the backlog is ordered by whoever complained most recently.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `intent_covered`, `accuracy_state`, `verified_against_version`


> Products move. An article that was correct against last quarter's build and is still being served confidently is worse than no article, because it converts a customer who was about to succeed into a customer who followed our instructions and failed. The version it was verified against is therefore not metadata here, it is the article's expiry date.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`

Requires `blast_radius`, `is_customer_visible`


> In a product business the first question of an incident is not how broken it is but how many people can see it broken. Blast radius decides whether this is a queue event or a broadcast event, and those two have opposite correct first actions.
